questions.q: How does the Lord express his anger because of Jeremiah’s rebellion?
questions.a: He has taken away the splendor of Israel and has humbled and brought down the cities of Judah.

questions.q: How does his anger affect Israel and Zion?
questions.a: The Lord removed all of Israel’s power, refused to protect them from their enemies, and he allowed them to be destroyed.

questions.q: How is the Lord’s anger shown?
questions.a: The Lord has become like an enemy; he destroyed the palaces and the temple and has rejected both the king and priest.

questions.q: Why does the enemy shout triumphantly?
questions.a: They shout triumphantly because the Lord abandoned his own holy place and has given the walls of the palace over to them.

questions.q: What has happened to the gates and bars of Zion?
questions.a: Her gates have come down, and Yahweh has destroyed and smashed the bars that held them shut.

questions.q: How do the elders and virgins show they are grieving?
questions.a: The elders sit on the ground, sprinkle their heads with dust while dressed in sackcloth. The virgins bow their heads down to the ground.
He weeps over the death and destruction of his people and because there is nothing for them to eat or drink.

questions.q: What do the mockers do as they pass by the city?
questions.a: They rejoice over the destruction by clapping their hands, hissing and shaking their heads with contempt, and grinding their teeth with hatred.

questions.q: What does the writer encourage the people of Jerusalem to do?
questions.a: He says they should cry out to the Lord and lift their hands to him continuously for the sake of their children.

questions.q: Why are the people begging for Yahweh’s mercy?
questions.a: They are begging for God’s mercy because they are extremely hungry and because their priests and prophets are being slaughtered.

questions.q: How does the writer describe the day of Yahweh’s wrath?
questions.a: On the day of Yahweh’s wrath, the enemy killed young and old, no one survived, and they showed no mercy.

commentary.text: Lamentation for the misery of Jerusalem.

Lam. 2:1-9 A sad representation is here made of the state of God's church, of Jacob and Israel; but the notice seems mostly to refer to the hand of the Lord in their calamities. Yet God is not an enemy to his people, when he is angry with them and corrects them. And gates and bars stand in no stead when God withdraws his protection. It is just with God to cast down those by judgments, who debase themselves by sin; and to deprive those of the benefit and comfort of sabbaths and ordinances, who have not duly valued nor observed them. What should they do with Bibles, who make no improvement of them? Those who misuse God's prophets, justly lose them. It becomes necessary, though painful, to turn the thoughts of the afflicted to the hand of God lifted up against them, and to their sins as the source of their miseries.

Lam. 2:10-22 Causes for lamentation are described. Multitudes perished by famine. Even little children were slain by their mother's hands, and eaten, according to the threatening, Deut. 28:53. Multitudes fell by the sword. Their false prophets deceived them. And their neighbours laughed at them. It is a great sin to jest at others' miseries, and adds much affliction to the afflicted. Their enemies triumphed over them. The enemies of the church are apt to take its shocks for its ruins; but they will find themselves deceived. Calls to lamentation are given; and comforts for the cure of these lamentations are sought. Prayer is a salve for every sore, even the sorest; a remedy for every malady, even the most grievous. Our business in prayer is to refer our case to the Lord, and leave it with him. His will be done. Let us fear God, and walk humbly before him, and take heed lest we fall.
